# Draft:Felix Warneken

Felix Warneken is a German-American developmental psychologist known for his research on the origins of altruism, cooperation, and early prosocial behavior in children. His work has received significant coverage in major international newspapers, radio broadcasts, and science magazines, including The New York Times, The Washington Post, NPR, and Scientific American, where journalists highlighted his contributions to understanding how and why infants spontaneously help others.
Warneken is a Professor of Psychology at the University of Michigan, where he directs the Social Minds Lab. His research and academic trajectory have also been profiled in institutional news outlets such as the Harvard Gazette and University of Michigan News, which reported on his awards and public recognition.
Early life and education
Warneken received his doctoral training at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany. As a graduate student, he began conducting comparative work examining early helping behavior in children and young chimpanzees, laying the foundation for his later research into the developmental origins of cooperation.
Academic career
Following his doctoral work, Warneken remained at the Max Planck Institute as a research scientist before joining the faculty at Harvard University. His appointment and leadership of new cooperation-focused research groups were noted in science-oriented institutional press.
He later moved to the University of Michigan, where he continues his research on social cognition, altruism, and prosocial development in early childhood.
Research and contributions
Early altruism and public reception
Warneken's early research showing that human infants spontaneously help unfamiliar adults attracted widespread media attention. In a widely cited experiment, toddlers watched an adult struggle with tasks such as picking up a dropped object or opening a cabinet, and many children intervened without prompting or reward. The New York Times described these findings as reshaping assumptions about early moral development, while The Washington Post and NPR reported on how the studies compared helping behaviors in children and young chimpanzees.
Intrinsic motivation and the effects of rewards
Warneken also studied how external rewards influence children's motivation to help. Scientific American summarized his findings, noting that rewarding toddlers for helping can paradoxically reduce their willingness to help later on. The article highlighted the broader implications for parenting, education, and theories of intrinsic motivation.
Fairness, cooperation, and cultural research
Beyond helping, Warneken has collaborated on studies examining fairness norms, resource sharing, and how cooperation develops across different societies. This work has been referenced in institutional award announcements and summarized in public-facing science communication outlets.
Recognition and media coverage
Warneken’s work has been featured in multiple high-profile science news publications and radio programs. Journalists have interviewed him about the evolutionary and developmental roots of altruism, discussed the scientific impact of his findings, and examined how his studies challenge traditional ideas about early childhood behavior. His research has also been acknowledged through early career awards and institutional honors reported in secondary sources such as the Harvard Gazette and University of Michigan press releases.
Selected publications
* Warneken, F., & Tomasello, M. (2006). Altruistic helping in human infants and young chimpanzees. Science, 311(5765), 1301–1303.
* Warneken, F., & Tomasello, M. (2008). Extrinsic rewards undermine altruistic tendencies in 20-month-olds. Developmental Psychology, 44(6), 1785–1788.
* Warneken, F., Hare, B., Melis, A. P., Hanus, D., & Tomasello, M. (2007). Spontaneous altruism by chimpanzees and young children. PLoS Biology, 5(7), e184.
* Warneken, F. (2015). Precocious prosociality: Why do young children help? Child Development Perspectives, 9(1), 1–6.
